title: Philip Neri (1515–1595)
hookLine: the laughing saint of Rome, who taught with jokes and music
last: A BAD NIGHT IN A BAD INN.

lines: A READING, A QUESTION, A SONG.
cards: An upstairs room in Rome, crowded in the afternoon. Young men from the shops and the banks, a few priests, some students, sitting on benches. Someone reads a page from a saint's life.
A priest in a worn cassock asks what they made of it, and the talk goes around the room. Then someone sings. More talk, and somebody laughs.
Nobody here is a monk. Nobody took a vow to come. The priest is Philip Neri, and the room gave its name to today's word: Oratory.

teach.h: A LAYMAN IN THE STREETS OF ROME.
teach.b: Philip came to Rome from Florence as a young layman and spent years praying in churches and, tradition says, in the catacombs by night, and talking with anyone in the streets.
He became a priest later, and he never stopped talking with people.
Then, the room. An oratory is a place of prayer, smaller than a church.
Philip's gatherings grew so large they needed one, and the group that ran them became the Congregation of the Oratory: priests living together without vows, held only by charity. Then, the music.
Philip wanted the meetings to be something people looked forward to.
Musicians sang hymns and spiritual songs in the language of the street, so a shopkeeper could follow along. And the jokes. Tradition remembers Philip as the laughing saint.

teach.h: HALF A BEARD, AND THE FEATHERS.
teach.b: Stories say he shaved half his beard, or read silly books in front of important visitors, so nobody would take him for holy. In one, a woman confesses to gossip.
He tells her to pluck a chicken while walking through the streets, then go back and gather every feather. She can't, of course. That, he says, is what gossip is like.
Whether every story happened or not, the laughter was the point: it kept him humble and kept sadness from settling in.
Some readers hear his spirit in a line from Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice." For Philip, joy was not a reward for being holy. It was part of the road.

how: Oratorian communities in cities around the world still hold gatherings of prayer, talk and music in Philip Neri's style, and the priests live together without vows.

games.q: you're Philip. a woman confesses that she gossips. what do you tell her to do?
o: say some prayers and go in peace.
pluck a chicken through the streets, then go back and gather every feather.
games.why: in the story, she can't gather the feathers, and that's the lesson: words, once scattered, don't come back.

practice: Smile a little, even if it feels silly, and think of someone who could use a lighter day. What makes them laugh: a memory you share, a ridiculous photo, a joke that's on you, not on anyone else?
If you pray, thank God for laughter, and for them; if you don't, simply enjoy picturing their face when it lands.

wordCard.voice: Oratory. A place of prayer, and the name of Philip Neri's community in Rome, born from crowded afternoons of reading, talk and music.

orig.note: Latin: a place of prayer, a small chapel. Philip's community took its name from the room where they met.
